The Liber Abaci, "Book of Calculation", is a Latin book on arithmetic written in 1202 by Leonardo of Pisa, known later as Fibonacci. It brought the Hindu-Arabic numerals, 0 to 9 with place value, to the merchants of Europe.

Leonardo's father was a customs official for Pisa at Bugia, today's Béjaïa in Algeria. There the boy learned to reckon with the numerals that Muslim scholars such as al-Khwarizmi had taken from India, a passage shown on the chart as Indian numerals reach Baghdad. He travelled round the Mediterranean to learn more.

The book teaches how to write and add numbers, multiply, work fractions and convert currencies, weights and measures, with many practical problems about profit, partnership and interest. One puzzle about breeding rabbits gives the number series later named after him.

The new numbers spread slowly, through "abacus schools" that trained the sons of Italian merchants. Over the following centuries they replaced Roman numerals in trade and bookkeeping, helping the rise of banking in cities like Venice and Florence.
